subject: Economics and Business

syllabus: Australian Curriculum: Economics and Business, Version 9.0, Year 8

points.title: Relevant and reliable sources
points.brief: A relevant source is about your question. A reliable one comes from an expert or official body, is recent, and backs its claims with evidence.

points.title: Finding trends in economic data
points.brief: A trend is the general direction data moves over time, such as rising prices over five years, even if some years go against it.

points.title: Costs and benefits for different groups
points.brief: A decision can help one group and cost another, so weigh its effects on consumers, workers, businesses and government separately.

points.title: Using economic terms in explanations
points.brief: A clear explanation uses the right terms, such as demand and opportunity cost, and supports each claim with data from a named source.

points.title: What a market is
points.brief: A market is any place or way buyers and sellers come together to trade, from a weekend market to an online store or the share market.

points.title: Sectors of the economy
points.brief: Households, businesses, the financial sector and government all take part in the market, buying, selling, saving, lending and taxing.

points.title: The circular flow of income
points.brief: Households sell their labour to businesses for income, and spend that income on businesses' goods and services, so money flows around the economy.

points.title: How markets answer the economic questions
points.brief: In a market economy, buyers and sellers trading freely decide what is produced, how it is produced and who gets it.

points.title: Demand
points.brief: Demand is how much of a product buyers want and can afford at each price. As price rises, people usually buy less.

points.title: Supply
points.brief: Supply is how much of a product sellers will offer at each price. As price rises, sellers usually offer more.

points.title: The equilibrium price
points.brief: The market price settles where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. Above it, unsold stock builds up; below it, there are shortages.

points.title: What changes a price
points.brief: Prices change with supply, demand, costs of making a product and competition, as petrol prices change with oil prices and how many stations compete.

points.title: Prices direct resources
points.brief: When a product's price rises, making it becomes more profitable, so businesses move resources into producing more of it.

points.title: Gaps and niches in the market
points.brief: Businesses look for needs nobody is meeting well, or small groups of buyers with special wants, called a niche.

points.title: Innovation
points.brief: Innovation is a new or better product or way of working, such as electric cars or home solar batteries, which can open new markets.

points.title: Technology and new business models
points.brief: Apps and the internet let businesses work in new ways, such as ride sharing, food delivery and online shops with no shopfront.

points.title: Technology and jobs
points.brief: Technology removes some jobs, such as checkout work, and creates others, such as in software and data, so workers need new skills over time.

points.title: Casual and gig work
points.brief: More Australians work casual or gig jobs, which are flexible but often have no sick leave, holiday pay or certain hours.

points.title: Outsourcing and offshoring
points.brief: Outsourcing pays another business to do work. Offshoring moves work overseas where wages are lower.

points.title: A changing workforce
points.brief: Australia's workforce is changing with an older population, more women working, new workplace laws and businesses taking more social and environmental responsibility.

points.title: First Nations partnerships and cooperatives
points.brief: First Nations businesses often join partnerships or cooperatives to share resources and reach bigger markets in areas such as farming, fashion, design and tourism.

points.title: Cultural tourism
points.brief: First Nations-run cultural tourism shares stories, art and knowledge of Country with visitors, on terms the community sets.

points.title: Bush foods and products from Country
points.brief: Some First Nations businesses make food, skin care and medicines from native plants, drawing on knowledge held for thousands of years and protecting how it is used.

points.title: Barriers to markets
points.brief: Remote First Nations businesses can face high transport costs and little access to finance. Buying programs such as Supply Nation help them win contracts.

points.title: Why governments collect tax
points.brief: Governments collect tax to pay for services such as health, education, roads, defence and support payments.

points.title: Income tax
points.brief: Income tax is taken from what people earn. Australia has a tax-free threshold, and people on higher incomes pay a higher rate on each extra dollar.

points.title: Young people and tax
points.brief: Young workers need a tax file number, their employer takes tax from their pay, and after 30 June they lodge a tax return and may get some back.

points.title: The goods and services tax
points.brief: The GST is a 10 per cent tax added to the price of most goods and services. Some things, such as most fresh food, are left out.

points.title: Excise and import duties
points.brief: Excise is a tax on goods such as fuel, alcohol and tobacco, and import duties tax goods from overseas. Both raise prices and can change what people buy.

points.title: Short and long-term financial goals
points.brief: A short-term goal, such as new shoes, takes weeks or months. A long-term goal, such as a car, takes years and needs a savings plan.

points.title: Making a personal budget
points.brief: A budget lists income and expenses, separating fixed costs from changing ones, so you can see what is left to save.

points.title: Saving and interest
points.brief: Money kept in a savings account earns interest, so savings grow over time, faster when interest is earned on interest.

points.title: Business financial records
points.brief: An income statement shows profit or loss, a balance sheet shows what a business owns and owes, and a cash flow statement shows money in and out.

points.title: Business plans and borrowing
points.brief: A business plan sets goals and how to reach them, and lenders such as banks read it before lending money to start or grow a business.
